sources.news_title: Giudice blocca la fusione Paramount-Warner Bros. su richiesta degli stati
sources.text:
Un giudice federale in California ha temporaneamente bloccato la fusione tra Paramount Skydance Corporation e Warner Bros. Discovery Inc., accogliendo la richiesta di una coalizione di stati che sta facendo causa per impedire del tutto il consolidamento dei due colossi mediatici.
“Questioni serie”
La procuratrice generale di New York, Letitia James, insieme a quelle di altri 11 stati tra cui la California, hanno intentato la loro azione legale contro la fusione il 13 luglio, sostenendo che viola il Clayton Act del 1914 — una delle leggi antitrust fondamentali degli Stati Uniti. La richiesta di un’ordinanza restrittiva temporanea (TRO) per bloccare la fusione è arrivata il 17 luglio, ed è stata accolta lunedì. “Questa causa riguarda un fatto semplice: quando un’unica azienda controlla una quota massiccia delle nostre industrie cinematografiche e televisive, a soffrirne sono i lavoratori, gli artisti, le imprese e i consumatori,” ha dichiarato James in un comunicato diffuso dal suo ufficio. “La fusione illegittima di Paramount con Warner Bros. significherebbe biglietti del cinema più costosi, abbonamenti tv più costosi, meno opportunità per i lavoratori e meno notizie originali condivise con il pubblico in tutto il paese.”
Sebbene la decisione della giudice distrettuale statunitense Araceli Martínez-Olguín, che accoglie la richiesta di TRO degli stati ricorrenti, sospenda la fusione solo fino a quando non sarà emessa una sentenza definitiva nella causa, essa si basa sul fatto che gli stati “sollevano questioni serie nel merito della loro azione ai sensi del Clayton Act”.
Una fusione controversa
Paramount ha iniziato a presentare offerte non richieste per Warner Bros. nel settembre 2025 e, sebbene Warner Bros. le abbia all’epoca respinte, il consiglio di amministrazione dell’azienda ha messo la società all’asta un mese dopo, attirando offerte concorrenti da altri colossi dei media. Nei mesi successivi si è scatenato un tira e molla tra Netflix e Paramount, con quest’ultima che ha avuto la meglio grazie a un accordo da 110 miliardi di dollari per acquistare Warner Bros. a 31 dollari per azione a febbraio.
La maggior parte della quota di mercato dei media americani è controllata da cinque aziende — le cosiddette “big five” — ed è così da quasi quarant’anni. Sebbene i nomi siano cambiati e le acquisizioni abbiano fatto confluire varie case di produzione sotto l’uno o l’altro di questi conglomerati, il numero di grandi studi è rimasto invariato.
L’acquisizione di Warner Bros. da parte di Paramount eliminerebbe uno dei pilastri delle big five, lasciando gli americani con quattro aziende che controllano quasi l’80 percento dei media che consumano, e un settore preoccupato per i tagli ai posti di lavoro, oltre che per la qualità dei contenuti trasmessi (e su computer e smart TV).
Personalità dei media prendono posizione
Oltre 5.000 attori, sceneggiatori e registi hanno firmato una lettera aperta per opporsi all’accordo, sostenendo che ridurrebbe la concorrenza e penalizzerebbe il loro settore, già “sotto forte pressione”.
Anche l’indipendenza delle redazioni è una preoccupazione importante, dato che David Ellison, vicino a Trump e ora presidente di Paramount dopo la fusione con Skydance nel 2025, ha apportato grandi cambiamenti a CBS News, insediando figure favorevoli a Trump in posizioni chiave che hanno già bloccato contenuti critici verso le politiche del presidente. I drastici cambiamenti nella storica redazione hanno sollevato preoccupazioni su cosa potrebbe accadere alla CNN, di proprietà di Warner Bros., se Ellison dovesse ottenerne il controllo. Anderson Cooper, giornalista veterano che ha lasciato il programma 60 Minutes di CBS News a causa dei cambiamenti, starebbe valutando, secondo alcune fonti, un addio alla CNN qualora la fusione andasse in porto.
David Ellison ha promesso di “costruire una Hollywood più forte”, in un settore che ha perso decine di migliaia di posti di lavoro negli ultimi cinque anni, ma è stato meno chiaro riguardo ai contenuti giornalistici. L’ex conduttore della CNN Jim Acosta ha lanciato l’allarme in un’audizione organizzata dal senatore della California Adam Schiff lo scorso marzo sul tema della fusione. “Se questa fusione va in porto, le tutele scompaiono,” ha dichiarato ai rappresentanti eletti e agli addetti ai lavori del settore riuniti al municipio di Burbank. “Se continuiamo su questa strada, sarà la fine dell’industria dell’informazione. Abbiamo bisogno di opzioni mediatiche che non siano controllate dalle persone più ricche e potenti del paese.”

sources.text:
Oh, boy — here we go.
The fate of the $111 billion Paramount–Warner Bros. merger could come down to a single federal judge, who has temporarily blocked the proposed deal, giving the 12-state coalition more time to pursue its antitrust challenge.
Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a 14-day temporary restraining order after finding that the states had raised serious questions about whether the merger could violate antitrust laws. Paramount and Warner Bros. will remain separate companies while the court considers whether to issue a longer preliminary injunction.
Take note that this is just 14 days—David Ellison is desperately hoping it doesn’t go any further. That’s because if the Paramount–Skydance/Warner Bros. Discovery merger is delayed beyond September 30, Paramount Skydance will have to pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders a “ticking fee” of roughly $6.8M .. per day. Yikes.
The next major step is a hearing on August 3 over whether to extend the block through the antitrust case. In merger disputes, that decision is often the whole ballgame: if the deal is allowed to close, it’s extremely difficult to unwind later. If a preliminary injunction is granted, however, mergers frequently fall apart before ever reaching trial.
However, the biggest takeaway for me is this: the judge signaled she was skeptical of Paramount’s argument that benefits in the streaming market could outweigh competitive harms in other markets, noting that courts generally do not allow efficiencies in one market to justify reduced competition in another. It’s a sign that the future of this merger has been granted over to a judge that’s not on the side of Paramount/Skydance.
This all comes just over a week after a coalition of 12 states filed an antitrust lawsuit seeking to block the proposed $111 billion merger between Paramount/Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal had already been approved by the Department of Justice last month. The coalition includes the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Washington.
From the outside looking in, there’s no doubt in my mind that this merger, like so many things these days, has become a blue-versus-red battle. The politics surrounding the deal now seem just as influential as the business and antitrust questions. We must also remember that the acquisition of CNN is part of this merger, and the fear among blue states is that David Ellison could very well turn it into a conservative outlet.

Paramount (PSKY) Shares Dip After Court Halts $110B Warner Bros. Discovery Deal
sources.text:
Key Takeaways
- A federal judge in California granted a 14-day temporary restraining order halting the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger
- Twelve states, spearheaded by California, filed the antitrust challenge on July 13 claiming anticompetitive concerns
- The coalition contends the $110 billion transaction would establish a dominant media entity capable of inflating consumer prices
- An August 3 hearing will determine if the temporary block becomes a longer-term injunction
- Paramount shares declined approximately 1.4% while Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) fell about 1.5% after the ruling
The proposed $110 billion combination between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery hit a major roadblock Monday, threatening the companies’ goal of finalizing the transaction by July’s end. A federal judge in California granted a temporary restraining order that halts the merger proceedings.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín delivered the 14-day pause following requests from twelve states headed by California, who contended the deal poses serious threats to market competition. The announcement triggered a roughly 1.4% slide in Paramount shares, with Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) experiencing a comparable 1.5% decline.
Paramount Skydance Corporation Class B Common Stock, PSKY
The multi-state coalition initiated their antitrust legal action on July 13 in Oakland’s federal courthouse. Their central complaint: the merged entity would accumulate excessive influence over the film and television landscape, ultimately driving up costs for viewers.
State Coalition Highlights Irreversible Consequences
Timing formed a critical component of the states’ argument. They emphasized that permitting the transaction to proceed — even on a provisional basis — would enable Paramount to commence workforce reductions and exchange confidential proprietary data with Warner Bros. Discovery.
Such measures, according to the states’ position, would prove virtually irreversible should a court eventually determine the merger violates antitrust regulations. Judge Martínez-Olguín found sufficient merit in this reasoning to implement an immediate pause pending further proceedings.
The court has set August 3 as the date for a comprehensive hearing to assess whether the temporary prohibition should remain in effect throughout the antitrust litigation.
Paramount Contests the Legal Challenge
Paramount has responded forcefully to the restraining order. The company maintains that the states’ legal filing fundamentally distorts well-established antitrust principles.
Company representatives further contend that stalling the transaction would inflict damage on entertainment industry professionals — workers who have already endured significant upheaval in recent years.
Under CEO David Ellison’s leadership, the Warner Bros. Discovery combination represents a cornerstone initiative aimed at repositioning Paramount as a legitimate competitor to streaming giants Netflix and Disney.
Different valuations place the merger between $81 billion and $110 billion, with the disparity reflecting varying treatments of assumed obligations. Regardless of the precise figure, this ranks among the most substantial media consolidations in contemporary history.
While California spearheaded the initiative, eleven additional states joined the legal action, lending it considerable geographical breadth and political significance.
Should the court approve a preliminary injunction during the August 3 proceedings, the companies would face a prohibition on completing the merger throughout the entire antitrust case — potentially extending many months into the future.
The current 14-day restriction has already forced Paramount beyond its targeted late-July completion timeline.
WBD stock registered declines ranging from 2.33% to 2.44% across various trading reports on Monday.

sources.news_title: Judge Temporarily Blocks Paramount’s $110 Billion Warner Bros. Discovery Merger
sources.text:
Hollywood’s relentless consolidation has finally hit a judicial roadblock. A federal judge has ordered a 14-day halt to Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, giving a coalition of 12 states more time to pursue its antitrust challenge against the deal.
U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted the temporary restraining order Monday after California. She will hold a hearing on August 3 to consider a preliminary injunction that could prevent the companies from merging while the lawsuit proceeds—a process that could take months to resolve.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta leads the coalition, which filed suit on July 13. Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Washington have joined California in the challenge.
The states contend that the transaction violates Section 7 of the Clayton Act by reducing competition across three markets: wide-release theatrical distribution, blockbuster film distribution, and basic cable television distribution. Their complaint alleges that the combined company would control approximately 30% of the market for anticipated top-grossing films and gain increased bargaining power over theater owners and cable providers.
That concentration, the states argue, could produce higher prices and fewer movies and television programs while leaving exhibitors and cable companies with less negotiating leverage. They also warned the court that Paramount could begin integrating operations and eliminating jobs immediately after closing, creating changes that would be difficult to reverse if the acquisition were later found unlawful.
Paramount has rejected the states’ market definitions and characterized the lawsuit as a distorted application of antitrust law. Its lawyers argue that theatrical competition now extends beyond Hollywood’s five legacy studios, pointing to releases from Amazon MGM Studios, Apple, Lionsgate, A24, and NEON as evidence that other distributors can compete successfully.
The company also claims the merger would strengthen its ability to compete against Netflix, Amazon, and other technology-backed entertainment companies. Paramount maintains that further delays would hurt an industry already battered by years of production contractions and job losses.
The temporary order does not determine whether the merger itself is illegal. It preserves the companies’ current separation until Martínez-Olguín can consider the states’ request for a longer injunction. Paramount had already offered to delay closing voluntarily if the court agreed to hold an expedited preliminary-injunction hearing.
Time carries a steep price for David Ellison’s company. If the transaction remains unfinished after September 30, Paramount must pay Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders a ticking fee of 25 cents per share for every additional day—approximately $7 million daily.
The Trump administration’s Department of Justice has already closed its antitrust investigation without challenging the acquisition. That federal decision does not prevent state attorneys general from mounting their own challenge under federal antitrust law.
The Writers Guild of America has filed a separate lawsuit seeking to stop the merger, arguing that combining two major employers would reduce writing opportunities, suppress compensation, and accelerate the industry’s contraction. The WGA case has also been assigned to Martínez-Olguín but has not been consolidated with the states’ lawsuit.
The merger would unite Paramount Pictures, CBS, Showtime, Nickelodeon, MTV, Comedy Central, BET, and Paramount+ with Warner Bros., HBO, HBO Max, CNN, DC Studios, Discovery, TNT, TBS, Food Network, HGTV, Cartoon Network, and Adult Swim. It would also bring “Harry Potter,” “Game of Thrones,” “Batman,” “Superman,” and the DC universe under the same corporate roof as “Top Gun,” “Mission: Impossible,” “Star Trek,” “SpongeBob SquarePants,” and “Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.”
Whether Ellison gets to assemble that unprecedented Hollywood empire now depends on a legal fight that moves into its next consequential stage on August 3.
